extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry/dramatic composition (poets, playwrights, literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic (and epic) poetry: requirements for plot unity, magnitude/length, the roles of reversal/recognition/passion, and the formal parts of a tragedy (prologue, episodes, choral odes, exit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity / Wholeness of the Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Totum est autem cui est initium et medium et finem. (The whole is that which has a beginning, a middle and an end.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plot must have a clear beginning, middle, and end; the parts must follow each other causally and be ordered so that removing or altering a part corrupts the whole. The imitation in a work should represent a single complete action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Appropriate Length
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabula debet habere magnitudinem aliquam. (The imitation ought to have some magnitude.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work must have sufficient magnitude for its events to be memorable and to accomplish an entire action; length should be enough to make the action easily apprehended (e.g., traditional practical measures such as the clepsydra/time of performance are noted). Magnitude is not simply size but that which allows a beginning, middle and end to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (One Principal Plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabula in opere est imitatio una unius et huius totius. (A play is the imitation of one action, one whole.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot should be a single, unified action rather than an aggregation of unrelated episodes; the whole should cohere toward one main action or outcome rather than multiple disconnected actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal Necessity and Probability of Events
rubrics_metrics.description: Res oportet esse probabiliter vel necessario; non quae accidunt casu. (Events should occur by necessity or probability, not by accident.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events ought to follow from prior events by necessity or likelihood; improbable or wholly accidental incidents reduce the quality of the imitation. Distinguish 'being for the sake of something' (causal aim) from 'being after something' (chronology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of Universals (Poetry vs. History)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poesis magis philosophica... universa; historia dicit particularia. (Poetry deals with universals; history with particulars.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should represent what may happen generally or necessarily (the universal), not only singular, particular facts; the poet's art deals in what is typical/possible, making it more philosophical than simple historical report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Use of Names and Particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: In tragoedia haerebant nominibus quae fuere... non ponunt quaelibet nomina. (Tragedy tends to adhere to names/known persons; comedy composes differently.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not indiscriminately insert arbitrary particulars; names and particulars in tragedy often tie to known states or traditional expectations and should be used to support plausibility rather than distract with irrelevant singularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Composite Plot (Inclusion of Reversal and Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplex est quod caret ratiocinatione vel circumvolutione; compositum habet transitum cum ratiocinatione vel circumvolutione. (Simple plots lack reversal/recognition; composite plots include them.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composite plots that include peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition) and connected reasoning tend to be superior; define whether the plot is simple or composite and use reversal/recognition deliberately to enhance effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (Peripeteia / Circumvolutio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumvolutio est mutatio in contrarium rerum quas faciunt. (A reversal is a change to the opposite of what seemed intended.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reversal should be plausible (probable or necessary) and arise from the plot's own constitution; it is often paired with recognition and can create delight when it transforms fortune convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratiocinatio... transitio ab inscientia ad scientiam... et recognitionis genera. (Recognition is transition from ignorance to knowledge; tied to inference.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition is most effective when surprising and beneficial (mirabilior et melior); best forms involve the agent recognizing before acting or at a climactic moment. Recognition paired with reversal intensifies tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination / Inference (Logos leading to Knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratiocinatio significat transitio ab inscientia ad scientiam quae est circa res. (Inference is the transition from ignorance to knowledge about some matter.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratiocination (a chain of reasoning) can appear in plots to effect recognition or to change the course of events; it need not be limited to human agents and can be structured to produce admiration when well executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion / Pathos as Third Part
rubrics_metrics.description: Passio est actio corrumpens vel angens... casus mortis et poenae et miseriae. (Passion is the action that brings about suffering—death, punishment, misery.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pathos should be used to arouse pity and fear; the suffering must fit the plot and be caused by events in the action (not arbitrary), producing the emotional responses proper to tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of Tragedy: Prologue, Episodes, Choral Odes, Exit
rubrics_metrics.description: Partes tragoediae sunt prologus introductio... exitus; chori sunt pars universalis tragoediae. (Tragedy comprises prologue, introduction, episodes, choral odes/stasima, exit.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy should employ these parts coherently: prologue/introduction, choral transitions (stasima) that serve as melodic medium, episodes, and an exit; these are commonly shared elements and should be proportioned by measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and Integration of the Chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: Chorus est medium melodiae totius chori; partes scaenae et transitus chori sunt pars universalis. (The chorus is the medium of the chorus's melody; choral parts are universal parts of tragedy.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chorus must be integrated into the action, providing transitions and melodic interludes that advance or reflect the plot, rather than being mere spectacle; the exit is also part of the whole structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to Arouse Pity and Fear (Catharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opus tragicum esse imitationem... ratiocinatio et circumvolutio erit misericordia aut timor. (Tragedy imitates actions that produce pity and fear.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose episodes and character situations to elicit pity and fear in the audience; not every pleasurable effect is appropriate—tragedy should produce an apt blend of these emotions rather than simple delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events Should Be Likely or Necessary (Avoid Casualness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex iis quae dicta sunt non esse operis poetae, sed illud tantum esse circum qualia occurrant sive possibile ex iis probabiliter, sive quae sunt necessaria. (The poet's work concerns what is within the realm of possibility or necessity, not mere accident.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base the plot on occurrences that are purely accidental or casual; events framed as the consequence of prior causes (probable or necessary) are more admired and appropriate for poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of Terrible and Pitiable Actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositio tragoediae debet esse... ex rebus terribilibus tristibus, et esse imitator horum. (Tragedy should be composed of terrible and lamentable things.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic plots should concern grave misfortunes, suffering, and morally weighty reversals (terror and pity), not trivial matters; such subject matter best fits the tragic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Error (Hamartia) over Moral Vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Non esse debet mutari ab felicitate in infelicitatem propter laborem sed propter errorem. (The change from good fortune to misfortune should come from error rather than from vice or moral depravity.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer protagonists who fall through error/mistake rather than through mere wickedness; this yields greater pity/fear and avoids making the outcome merely just punishment. The error should be significant and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Believability of Transitions (From Prosperity to Misery and Back)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quum fit in his quae sunt necessario unum post alterum, evadit in prosperitatem quae fit post infelicitatem vel mutatur infelicitas in successum; erit magnitudinis terminus sufficiens. (Sequenced necessary events can justify dramatic reversals.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitions of fortune should be credible within the plot's causal logic; when a chain of necessary events leads from prosperity to disaster (or vice versa), the magnitude and terminus of the plot are sufficient and satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Should Work by Hearing (Not Only Spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decet componi fabulam hoc modo sine visu ut audiens res contremiscat. (A poet should compose so that the hearer trembles even without seeing the spectacle.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good tragedy should produce emotional effect through its composition and language alone; dependence on visual spectacle for the tragic impact is a sign of weaker poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts Must Be Proportioned and Measure-determined
rubrics_metrics.description: Partes secundum mensuram et in quot partes oporteat dividi compendium haec sunt. (Parts should be divided according to measure and proportion.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how many and which parts a tragedy requires and proportion them appropriately; the division of parts (prologues, choruses, episodes) should serve the whole and be measured, not arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for Composed/Planned Events over Purely Fortuitous Ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Quae sunt casualia ex iis putantur ea esse mirabiliora quotquot videntur esse consilio. (Casual events are regarded as more surprising when they appear to be the result of design.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even events that seem surprising should feel designed by the plot's internal logic; the appearance of planning enhances admiration, whereas true randomness undermines poetic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot Constituents: Recognition, Reversal, and Suffering are the Three Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Hae quas memoravimus sunt duae partes fabulae scil. ratiocinatio et circumvolutio; et tertia pars est passio. (The parts of plot include inference, reversal, and suffering.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing a complex plot, ensure ratiocination (inference/argument leading to knowledge), circumvolutio (reversal of fortune), and pathos (suffering) are present and arranged to produce the intended tragic affect.
